However, no suitable therapy exists to treat these pain syndromes. Our laboratory explored novel potential therapeutic strategies using a suitable composition of neurotrophic factors and active peptide fragments-Cerebrolysin (Ever Neuro Pharma, Austria) in alleviating neuropathic pain induced spinal cord pathology in a rat model. Neuropathic pain was produced by constrictions of L-5 spinal sensory nerves for 2\\u201310 weeks period. In one group of rats cerebrolysin (2.5 or 5 ml/kg, i.v.) was administered once daily after 2 weeks until sacrifice (4, 8 and 10 weeks). Ag, Cu and Al NPs (50 mg/kg, i.p.) were delivered once daily for 1 week. Pain assessment using mechanical (Von Frey) or thermal (Hot-Plate) nociceptive showed hyperalgesia from 2 weeks until 10 weeks progressively that was exacerbated following Ag, Cu and Al NPs intoxication in nerve lesioned groups. Immunohistochemistry of albumin and GFAP exhibited a close parallelism with BSCB leakage that was aggravated by NPs following nerve lesion. Light microscopy using Nissl stain exhibited profound neuronal damages in the cord. ANOVA followed by Dunnett’s test for multiple group comparison was done using one control group using commercial software StatView 5 (Abacus Concept, USA) on a Macintosh computer in Classic Environment. A p-value less than 0.05 was considered significant.

## Results
[Table 2: Physiological variables in neuropathic pain in control, sham and nanoparticles exposed group in the rat and their modification with cerebrolysin treatment — 26 rows x 9 cols; see tables]
[Table 3: Mechanical electronic Von Frey stimulation on paw withdrawal response or thermal radiant heat stimulus (52 °C) to tail flick tests in nerve lesion in control or nanoparticles from metals Ag, Cu or Al in rats and their modification with Cerebrolsyin treatment — 26 rows x 4 cols; see tables]
[Table 4: Blood-Spinal cord barrier (BSCB) breakdown and edema formation in the cord following neuropathic pain with nanoparticle intoxication in the rat and neuroprotection with cerebrolysin treatment — 26 rows x 10 cols; see tables]
[Table 5: Measurement of albumin, glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), myelin basic protein (MBP) and heat shock protein (HSP 72 kD) in the spinal cord following nerve lesion and intoxication with Ag and Cu nanoparticle and their modification with cerebrolysin treatment — 20 rows x 10 cols; see tables]
[Table 6: Measurement of tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), interleukin-6 (IL-6), IL-4 and IL-10 in the spinal cord following nerve lesion and intoxication with Ag and Cu nanoparticle and their modification with cerebrolysin treatment — 20 rows x 10 cols; see tables]

## Physiological Variables
Changes in the body weight, rectal temperature, heart rate and respiration rate were examined in control, sham and nerve lesioned rats with or without nanoparticles intoxication. The arterial pH, blood gases and mean arterial blood pressure (MABP) were examined in all groups. The results are shown in Table 2.

The body weight in nerve lesioned animals increased significantly after 4 weeks in a progressive manner and this effect was also seen following nanoparticles intoxications and cerebrolysin treatments in all groups (Table 2).

However, rectal temperature showed a slight decrease from the control or sham group following nerve lesion with or without nanoparticles treatments. On the other hand, cerebrolysin treatment attenuated this decrease in nerve lesion and nanoparticles intoxication (Table 2).

Chronic nerve lesion significantly increased heart rate as compared to controls or sham group. This increase in heart rate after nerve lesion is further potentiated with nanoparticles intoxication (Table 2). Treatment with cerebrolysin attenuated this increase in heart rate in nerve lesion with and without nanoparticles intoxication (Table 2).

Respiration rate after nerve lesion in saline treated rats showed significant decrease after 10 weeks whereas, nanoparticles intoxication significantly raised the respiration rate during 8–10 weeks of nerve lesion (Table 2)- Cerebrolysin treatment significantly attenuated this increase in respiration rate in nanoparticles intoxicated nerve lesioned arts in Ag and Cu group. However, Al nanoparticles showed significant increase in cerebrolysin treated nerve lesioned group (Table 2).

The MABP increased significantly in nerve lesioned rats progressively and this effect was further enhanced with nanoparticles intoxication and cerebrolysin treatment significantly attenuated this rise in MABP (Table 2). The arterial pH exhibited slight decrease in nerve lesioned group with or without nanoparticles intoxication; however, the values were not significantly altered (Table 2). The PaO2 significantly increased after nerve lesion that was exacerbated in Ag and Cu nanoparticles administered group except in Al nanoparticles exposed rats after nerve lesion (Table 2). Cerebrolysin treatment markedly thwarts this rise in PaO2 following nerve lesion with or without exposure (Table 2). On the other hand, PaCO2 significantly elevated after nerve lesion and further exacerbated with nanoparticles exposure in nerve lesion group. Cerebrolysin treatment significantly attenuated this increase in PaCO2 in nerve lesion with or without nanoparticles intoxication (Table 2).

## Pain Hypersensitivity
Control and sham treated animals with or without nanoparticles treatment did not show hypersensitivity to mechanical or thermal stimulations.

Pain hypersensitivity was measured in nerve lesioned group with or without nanoparticles exposure using mechanical stimulation or thermal stimulation. Von Frey hair stimulation weight and latency of paw withdrawal significantly reduced in nerve lesioned rats progressively with time (Table 3). This effect was further exacerbated with nanoparticles exposure. Treatment with cerebrolysin significantly enhanced the weight of Von Frey hair with almost identical paw withdrawal latency in nerve lesioned group with or without nanoparticles intoxication (Table 3).

Likewise thermal radiant stimulus induced tail flick latency showed significant reduction in nerve lesioned group with or without nanoparticles exposure. However, cerebrolysin treatment significantly enhanced the tail flick latency following thermal stimulus in nerve lesioned rats with or without nanoparticles intoxication (Table 3).

## Blood-Spinal Cord Barrier Breakdown
Breakdown of the BSCB was measured using leakage of Evans blue albumin (EBA) and radioactive iodine in nerve lesioned rats with or without nanoparticles intoxication. The results are shown in Table 4. Nerve lesioned rats exhibited significant leakage of EBA and 131-I within the spinal cord segments T10-11 and L5-S2 progressively from 4 to 10 weeks of nerve lesion (Table 3). This breakdown of the BSCB to EBA and radioiodine was further exacerbated following nanoparticles exposure (Table 4). Treatment with cerebrolysin significantly attenuated the BSCB leakage of EBA or radioiodine in these segments after nerve lesion with or without nanoparticles exposure (Table 4).

## Spinal Cord Edema Formation and Volume Swelling
Leakage of serum proteins into the spinal cord induces edema formation and volume swelling. Thus, edema formation was measured using spinal cord water content and volume swelling (%ƒ) was calculated from the changes of water content as described earlier.

The results are shown in Table 4. Spinal nerve lesion significantly caused edema formation and volume swelling within the cord that was progressive over 4–10 weeks of nerve lesion. This effect was further enhanced with nanoparticles exposure (Table 4).

Treatment with cerebrolysin significantly attenuated edema formation and volume swelling in nerve lesioned group with or without nanoparticles exposure (Table 4).

## Biochemical Changes
We previously reported increased albumin and GFAP immunohistochemistry following chronic nerve lesion from 4 to 10 weeks that showed maximum increase at 10 weeks of nerve lesion. In this study, we measured albumin, GFAP, myelin basic protein (MBP) and heat shock protein 72 kD (HSP 72 kD) using ELISA. The results are shown in Table 5.

Nerve lesion significantly enhanced albumin levels in the spinal cord progressively from 4 to 10 weeks following the lesion. Intoxication of nanoparticles further enhanced the albumin levels within the spinal cord. Treatment with cerebrolysin significantly thwarted this increase in albumin level in the spinal cord segments after nerve lesion (Table 5).

On the other hand, GFAP Elisa exhibited also significant rise in the spinal cord of nerve lesioned group from 4th to 10th week progressively (Table 5). This was further exacerbated following nanoparticles intoxication in nerve lesioned groups (Table 5). However, cerebrolysin treatment significantly reduced GFAP levels within the spinal cord segments in both nanoparticles exposed group and normal nerve lesion rats (Table 5).

Measurement of MBP levels showed significant increase within the spinal cord as compared from the control or sham operated animals following nerve lesion. This increase in MBP denoting breakdown of myelin was seen 4 weeks after the nerve lesion that progressively increased throughout up to 10 weeks period (Table 5). Exposure of nanoparticles further exacerbated MBP levels within the spinal cord after nerve lesion. Interestingly, cerebrolysin treatment significantly attenuated myelin degradation after nerve lesion with or without nanoparticle exposure as is evident from reduction in MBP levels within the cord (Table 5).

Likewise the stress of chronic nerve lesion significantly enhanced HSP 72 kD protein levels within the spinal cord segments progressively from 4 weeks period to 10 weeks duration. Intoxication with nanoparticle exacerbated HSP 72 kD levels in the spinal cord segments after nerve lesion in animals (Table 5).

Treatment with cerebrolysin in nerve lesioned group either with nanoparticles exposure or without them significantly reduced the HSP 72 kD levels within the spinal cord (Table 5).

## Measurement of Cytokines in Nerve Lesion
The levels of both inflammatory and anti-inflammatory cytokines were measured within the spinal cord of control, sham and nerve lesioned group with or without nanoparticles exposure. The levels of TNF-α and IL-6 as inflammatory cytokines and IL-10 and IL-4 as anti-inflammatory cytokines are displayed in Table 6.

The results show that both inflammatory cytokine significantly increased within the spinal cord segments after nerve lesion from 4th to 10th week of survival in a progressive manner (Table 6). Intoxication with nanoparticle further enhanced the inflammatory cytokine after nerve lesion within the spinal cord segments significantly (Table 6).

The anti-inflammatory cytokine also enhanced after nerve lesion from 4th to 8th week but declined at 10th week of survival. On the other hand, nanoparticles exposure in nerve lesion resulted in further exacerbation from 4th to 10th week after nerve lesion in a progressive manner (Table 6).

Treatment with cerebrolysin significantly reduced the accumulation of inflammatory cytokines in the spinal cord after 10th week of nerve lesion. This effect was also seen in nerve lesioned group intoxicated with nanoparticles significantly with cerebrolysin (Table 6). Whereas cerebrolysin was able to enhance anti-inflammatory cytokines in the spinal cord significantly at 10th week after nerve lesioned group either with or without nanoparticles exposure (Table 6).

## Spinal Cord Morphology
Spinal cord morphology was examined using standard histopathological techniques and immunocytochemistry in nerve lesioned group intoxicated with nanoparticles. Semiquantitative analysis of data was also done on the spinal cord segments at T10, T12 and L5 in all groups.

## Neuronal Injury
Analysis of neuronal injury in Nissl or H&E stained 3-µm thick paraffin sections were counted for neuronal distortion, dark neurons or chromatolysis and counted in each segment by 3 independent observes. The median values were taken in account in 6 to 8 different animals and shown in Fig. 2. As seen within the graph the numbers of neuronal injury following nerve lesion in the T10, T12 and L5 segments is significantly increased as compared to the control group. This increase in neural injury is further exacerbated following Cu or Ag nanoparticles with nerve lesion (Fig. 2). There was a significant increase in neuronal injury after nerve lesion with or without nanoparticles after 8 and 10 weeks as compared to the 4 weeks lesion from the control group of different spinal cord segments (Fig. 2).

[Fig. 2: Upper panel; Shows neuronal distortion in nerve cells within the spinal cord segments of T10, T12 and L5 in control group and following nerve lesion 4, 8 and 10 weeks survival in the rat. Treatment with nanoparticles (NPs) Cu or Ag (50–60 nm) exacerbated neuronal injury or distortion at 4, 8 or 10 weeks from the nerve lesioned group significantly as compared from the controls. Treatment with Cu or Ag nanoparticles in nerve lesion shows a significant linear increase in neuronal injury in the T10, T12 and L5 segments following 4, 8 and 10 weeks survival. Ag nanoparticles has significant neuronal damages in the nerve lesioned group as compared with Cu treated nerve lesioned animals in the T10, T12 and L5 segments over the 4, 8 and 10 weeks period of nerve lesion. Lower panel: Shows cerebrolysin (CBL) treatment in nerve lesion (NL, 2.5 ml/kg, i.v.) significantly attenuated neuronal distortion whereas in nanoparticles treated group CBL (5 ml/kg, i.v.) significantly attenuated neuronal distortion in nanoparticles treated group of 10 weeks. Each point represents 6 to 8 rats. ANOVA followed by Dunnett’s test for multiple group comparison from respective controls. * = P < 0.01, ∆ = P < 0.05 For details see text]

A representative example of neuronal injury in the spinal cord segment is presented using Nissl staining (Fig. 3). As evident from the figure several damaged or distorted nerve cells are present within the spinal cord L5 segment that are significantly elevated with Ag nanoparticles or Cu nanoparticles at 10 weeks survival (Fig. 3). Cerebrolysin treatment in spinal nerve lesion intoxicated rats with Ag nanoparticles is significantly attenuated (Fig. 3).

[Fig. 3: Representative example of Nissl stained nerve cells within the spinal cord dorsal (a, b) horn and ventral horn (c, d) after 10 weeks of nerve lesion (a) and their exacerbation with Cu nanoparticles (CuNPs, (b) and Ag nanoparticle (AgNPs, c) and this effect was markedly attenuated by cerebrolysin (CBL, 5 ml/kg, i.v.) with AgNPs treated nerve lesioned rat (d). Several spinal nerve cells were distorted or damaged (arrows) within the dorsal horn (a) and this was further aggravated with CuNPs intoxication (arrows, b). Likewise, in the ventral horn also several neurons show distortion and perineuronal edema present in spongy or expanded neuropil subjected to AgNPs intoxication (arrows, c). Treatment with CBL markedly attenuated the distortion of spinal cord neurons (Ventral horn, d, arrows) and several neurons appear healthy within the neuropil (arrow, d). Paraffin Sect. 3 µm. Bars: a = 20 µm; b = 25 µm, c, d = 40 µm]

Treatment with cerebrolysin markedly attenuated nerve cell injury after nerve lesion (Figs. 2–4) intoxicated with Cu or Ag nanoparticles. A representative example of nerve cell injury in cerebrolysin treated group is shown in Figs. 3 and 4.

[Fig. 4: High power Light microscope (LM) images from right ventral horn of the T12 spinal cord after spinal nerve lesion associated with Ag or Cu nanoparticles intoxications and their neuroprotection with cerebrolysin treatment. Nerve lesion (NL) alone markedly distorted neurons (arrows, c) and this neuronal damage is further exacerbated with Cu (d) and Ag (b) nanoparticles (arrows). Ag nanoparticles induced greater neuronal injury (b) as compared to Cu nanoparticles (d). Treatment with cerebrolysin (CBL, a) in Ag nanoparticles intoxication markedly attenuated neuronal distortion (arrows). In general CBL treated group show compact neuropil with compact neuronal structure as compared to expansion of neuropil with severely distorted neurons with perineuronal edema and sponginess (b). H&E Stain on 3-µm thick paraffin sections, Bar = 30 µm]

## Albumin Immunoreactivity
Immunohistochemistry of endogenous albumin leakage within the spinal cord was performed in the identical spinal cord segments T10, T12 and L5 following nerve lesion with or without Cu or Ag nanoparticles intoxication (Fig. 5). Albumin positive cells in nerve lesion as compared to control and after nanoparticles Cu or Ag treatments are displayed in Figs. 6 and 7. As evident with these figures, there was a gradual increase in albumin leakage among the spinal cord segments progressively from the distant T10 segment to the adjacent T12 segment followed by the nerve lesioned segment L5. This increase in albumin positive cells was further exacerbated following Cu nanoparticles or Ag nanoparticles intoxication (Figs. 6 and 7). It appears that Ag nanoparticles intoxication induces higher leakage of albumin within the all spinal cord segments examined in nerve lesioned groups (Figs. 6 and 7).

[Fig. 5: Upper panel: Graphic representation of albumin positive immunoreactive cells within the spinal cord segments of T10, T12 and L5 in control and nerve lesioned rats after 4, 8 or 10 weeks survival periods. Treatment with nanoparticles (NPs) Cu or Ag (50–60 nm) exacerbated albumin leakage at 4, 8 or 10 weeks from the nerve lesioned group significantly. Treatment with Cu or Ag nanoparticles in nerve lesion shows a significant linear increase in albumin immunoreactive cells in the T10, T12 and L5 segments following 4, 8 and 10 weeks survival. Ag nanoparticles has significant higher leakage of albumin positive immunoreactive cell in the nerve lesioned group as compared with Cu treated nerve lesioned animals in the T10, T12 and L5 segments over the 4, 8 and 10 weeks period of nerve lesion. Lower Panel: Cerebrolysin (CBL) treatment in 10 weeks of spinal nerve lesion (NL) significantly thwarted albumin leakage in 2.5 ml/kg, i.v. whereas in nanoparticles intoxicated group 5 ml/kg (i.v.) CBL is able to significantly reduce albumin leakage after nerve lesion. The data are Mean ± SD of 6 to 8 rats. ANOVA followed by Dunnett’s test for multiple group comparison from respective controls. * = P < 0.01, ∆ = P < 0.05, For details see text]

[Fig. 6: Representative example of albumin positive immunoreactive cells within the spinal cord after 10 weeks of nerve lesion (a) and their exacerbation with Cu nanoparticles (CuNPs, (b) spinal cord Ag nanoparticle (AgNPs, c) and this effect was much less prominent after 4 weeks of nerve lesioned rat (d). Several albumin immunoreactive cells were distorted or damaged (arrows) within the spinal cord (a–d) and this was further aggravated with CuNPs or AgNPs intoxication (arrows, b, c). Paraffin Sect. 3 µm. Bars: a-d = 25 µm]

[Fig. 7: Representative example of cerebrolysin (CBL 5 ml/kg, i.v.) treated AgNPs intoxicated rat showing albumin positive immunoreactive cells within the spinal cord after 10 weeks of nerve lesion (a) as compared to untreated nerve lesioned rat with AgNPs (b). Several albumin immunoreactive cells were distorted or damaged (arrows) within the spinal cord (b) in AgNPs intoxication (arrows, b) and CBL treatment markedly reduced the magnitude of albumin positive cells and expansion of the cord (arrows, a). Paraffin Sect. 3 µm. Bars: a, b = 25 µm]

A representative example of albumin leakage in nerve lesion after 4 and 10 weeks of survival is shown in Figs. 6 and 7. The albumin leakage across the spinal cord in T10 segment is most pronounced after 10 weeks of nerve lesion. This increase in albumin leakage was further exacerbated in nerve lesioned group following intoxication with Cu or Ag nanoparticles at 10 weeks period (Fig. 7).

Cerebrolysin treatment in nerve lesioned group after 10 weeks in Ag nanoparticles intoxicated rats was markedly attenuated (Figs. 5–7) that also showed the reduction in cord expansion (Fig. 6).

## GFAP Immunohistochemistry
Using immunohistochemistry, GFAP was examined in the identical segments of the spinal cord of nerve lesioned rats and after intoxication with Cu or Ag nanoparticles. The number of GFAP positive cells was counted and shown in various groups in Fig. 8.

[Fig. 8: Upper panel: Graphic representation of glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) positive immunoreactive cells within the spinal cord segments of T10, T12 and L5 in control and nerve lesioned rats after 4, 8 or 10 weeks survival periods. Treatment with nanoparticles (NPs) Cu or Ag (50–60 nm) exacerbated albumin leakage at 4, 8 or 10 weeks from the nerve lesioned group significantly. Treatment with Cu or Ag nanoparticles in nerve lesion shows a significant linear increase in GFAP immunoreactive cells in the T10, T12 and L5 segments following 4, 8 and 10 weeks survival. Ag nanoparticles has significant higher reactive astrocytes as seen with GFAP in the nerve lesioned group as compared with Cu treated nerve lesioned animals in the T10, T12 and L5 segments over the 4, 8 and 10 weeks period as compared to control, nerve lesioned and nanoparticles (Cu or Ag) treated lesioned rats. Lower panel: Treatment with cerebrolysin in 10 weeks nerve lesion (NL) significantly attenuated GFAP activation (2.5 ml/kg, i.v.) while in nanoparticles exposed group CBK 5 ml/kg, i.v. is needed to reduce GFAP activation, The data are Mean ± SD of 6 to 8 rats at each point. ANOVA followed by Dunnett’s test for multiple group comparison from respective controls. * = P < 0.01, ∆ = P < 0.05. For details see text]

The number of GFAP positive astrocytes was enhanced progressively from 4 weeks of nerve lesion to 10 weeks survival period. There was a significant increase in numbers of GFAP positive cells from nerve lesioned group at various time periods following intoxication with Cu followed by Ag nanoparticles. This increase in the number of GFAP positive astrocytes was highest in L5 segment followed by adjacent T12 segment and the distant T10 spinal cord segment (Fig. 8).

A representative example of GFAP immunohistochemistry in nerve lesioned group of 4 and 8 weeks survival is shown in Fig. 9. As evident from the figure there was a massive increase in GFAP immunostaining at 8 weeks in T12 segment of the spinal cord as compared to the 4 weeks period of nerve lesion (Fig. 9) as compared to Sham operated group (Fig. 9). Intoxication with Cu nanoparticles further increased the GFAP immunoreactivity within the T12 spinal cord segment after 8 weeks of nerve lesion period (Fig. 9).

[Fig. 9: Representative example of glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) immunoreactive cells within the spinal cord dorsal horn after 8 weeks of nerve lesion (a) and their exacerbation with Cu nanoparticles (CuNPs, b) as compared to sham (c) and 4 weeks of nerve lesion (d). The magnitude and severity of GFAP immunoreactive cells (arrows) are markedly exacerbated with Cu NPs intoxication in nerve lesion after 8 weeks survival (b, arrows) and this effect was much less prominent after 4 weeks of nerve lesioned rat (d). Only a few GFAP positive cells are seen in sham lesioned rat after 8 weeks (c, arrow). Paraffin Sect. 3 µm. Bars: a–d = 35 µm]

Treatment with cerebrolysin markedly attenuated GFAP immunostaining within the spinal cord T12 segment after 10 weeks of nerve lesioned rat (Figs. 8 and 10). Also the effects of cerebrolysin treatment were prominent in the spinal cord after nerve lesion with Ag nanoparticles intoxication at this time in the T12 spinal cord segment (Figs. 8 and 10).

[Fig. 10: Representative example of glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) immunoreactive cells within the spinal cord ventral horn treated with cerebrolysin (CBL 5 ml/kg, i.v.) after 10 weeks of nerve lesion (a) and their exacerbation with Ag nanoparticles (AgNPs, b). The magnitude and severity of GFAP immunoreactive cells (arrows) are markedly reduced in nerve lesioned rats (a, arrows) and also thwarted GFAP immunoreaction following Ag NPs following nerve lesion (b, arrows). Thus, only some nerve fibers exhibit immunoreaction the spinal cord of nerve lesioned rat (a, arrows) or following AgNPs intoxication (b, arrows). Paraffin Sect. 3 µm. Bars: a, b = 40 µm]

## Ultrastructural Changes
Using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) spinal cord segments T12 and L5 were examined in the nerve lesioned rats after 10 weeks of survival with or without exposure to Ag or Cu nanoparticles. A representative example of T12 spinal cord segments in the nerve lesioned group after 10 weeks period is shown in Fig. 11. As evident from the figure several myelinated axons are distorted within the expanded neuropil showing edema and membrane vacuolation. Membrane vacuolation, edema and axonal damage are clearly seen within the neuropil of spinal cord segment T12 after 10 weeks of nerve lesion (Fig. 11d).

[Fig. 11: Representative example of transmission electron microscope images (TEM) showing ultrastructural changes in myelin vesiculation within spinal cord of sham (a), nerve lesioned rat after 10 weeks (b) and exacerbation myelin vesiculation with Ag nanoparticles (AgNPs, c) and associated neuropil exhibiting synaptic damage and membrane vacuolation after 10 weeks of nerve lesion (d). Only minimal distortion in myelin structure is seen in sham lesioned rat (a, arrows) whereas, nerve lesioned rat exhibited marked distortion of myelin (arrows) and membrane vacuolation (*) (b). AgNPs intoxication in nerve lesioned rat exacerbated myelin vesiculation (arrows, c) with membrane disruption (*) after 10 weeks o nerve lesion. Within the neuropil of nerve lesioned rat after 10 weeks signs of synaptic damage and membrane vacuolation (*) appears prominent (arrows, d). Ultrathin Sect. (50 nm) contrasted with lead citrate and uranyl acetate, Phillips 400 TEM, Bar = 1 µm]

Intoxication with Ag nanoparticles further exacerbated myelin vesiculation, edema formation and membrane disruption (Fig. 11).

On the other hand, treatment with cerebrolysin markedly preserved myelin vesiculation associated with Ag nanoparticles intoxication and reduced the membrane disruption or vacuolation after 10 weeks of nerve lesion (Fig. 11). Cerebrolysin treatment markedly reduced myelin vesiculation after nerve lesion as evident from Fig. 12. Cerebrolysin treatment reduces both myelin vesiculation and membrane vacuolation in nerve lesion intoxicated with Ag or Cu nanoparticles (Fig. 12).

[Fig. 12: High power Transmission Electro Microscope (TEM) images of spinal cord myelin vesiculation (arrow) and membrane vacuolation (*) from segment T12 following spinal nerve lesion 10 weeks dorsal horn associated with Ag (a) or Cu (c) intoxication and their modification with cerebrolysin (CBL) treatment (b, d). As seen with TEM micrograph that CBL treatment markedly reduced myelin vesiculation (arrow) and membrane vacuolation (*) following spinal nerve lesion. Ultrathin Sect. (50 nm) contrasted with lead citrate and uranyl acetate, Phillips 400 TEM, Bar = 1 µm]",

hypotheses.statement: Chronic constriction nerve lesion progressively induces hyperalgesia, blood-spinal cord barrier breakdown, cord edema and structural/biochemical cord pathology over 4-10 weeks.
hypotheses.provenance_quote: Pain assessment using mechanical (Von Frey) or thermal (Hot-Plate) nociceptive showed hyperalgesia from 2 weeks until 10 weeks progressively

hypotheses.statement: Intoxication with engineered Ag, Cu or Al nanoparticles (50-60 nm) exacerbates the behavioural, barrier, biochemical and structural consequences of nerve lesion.
hypotheses.provenance_quote: that was exacerbated following Ag, Cu and Al NPs intoxication in nerve lesioned groups

hypotheses.statement: Cerebrolysin treatment (2.5 or 5 ml/kg i.v.) attenuates hyperalgesia, BSCB disruption, edema, cytokine elevation and cord pathology, including in nanoparticle-intoxicated animals.
hypotheses.provenance_quote: Cerebrolysin treatment significantly reduced hyperalgesia and attenuated BSCB disruption, edema formation and cellular changes in nerve lesioned group.

findings.location: Table 1 (Experimental Protocol in Nerve Lesion), row Total column
findings.quote: Experiments were carried out on 348 male albino Wistar Rats
findings.notes: 3 of 18 per-group row totals in Table 1 exceed the sum of their own three assay-stream cells by exactly 2 animals each. The remaining 15 rows reconcile exactly. Animal counts must hold exactly, so tolerance was set to 0. The constant +2 offset in all three failures is consistent with transcription/editing error rather than a random arithmetic slip, but the direction is always toward over-stating the number of animals.

consequence.explanation: The per-group n that every significance test in Tables 2-6 depends on cannot be pinned down for these three groups, since the table gives two different answers for each.

findings.location: Table 1, Grand Total row against the assay columns above it
findings.quote: Experiments were carried out on 348 male albino Wistar Rats
findings.notes: Two of the three printed column Grand Totals are LOWER than the sum of the cells printed above them (106 vs 114; 112 vs 118). The Biochemical Analyses column reconciles exactly. Note the direction is opposite to the row-total errors, which over-state; these under-state.

consequence.explanation: The number of animals contributing to the physiological/pain measurements (Tables 2 and 3) and to the BSCB measurements (Table 4) is stated two ways that differ by 8 and 6 animals respectively.

findings.location: Table 1 grand total and Animals section ('348 male albino Wistar Rats')
findings.quote: Experiments were carried out on 348 male albino Wistar Rats

comparisons: vs sum of the 18 printed row Totals = 368

findings.notes: The paper's animal accounting yields THREE mutually inconsistent totals: the individual cells of Table 1 sum to 362; the printed per-group Total column sums to 368; and both the stated text figure and the printed Grand Total cell say 348. Only the last two agree with each other, and they agree only because 106 + 112 + 130 = 348 -- i.e. the grand total is internally consistent with the (incorrect) column totals rather than with the animals actually listed. All three numbers cannot describe the same experiment.

consequence.explanation: The headline sample size of the study -- 348 rats -- is not recoverable from the paper's own allocation table, which accounts for either 362 or 368 animals depending on which printed figures are added.

findings.location: Table 2, Respiration cycle/min, Nerve Lesion 4 wk (12 ± 9*) vs Control (14 ± 3)
findings.quote: Values are Mean ± SD of 6–8 rats at each point.
findings.notes: n was set to 8 per group, the TOP of the paper's stated 6-8 range, which is the assumption most favourable to the authors' significance claim; at n=6 the p-values would be larger still. The achievable two-tailed p across the entire rounding interval implied by the printed 0-decimal means and SDs is [0.354, 0.786], and one-tailed [0.177, 0.393]. p < 0.05 is unreachable under Welch's and Student's tests, one- or two-tailed. The paper's stated analysis was ANOVA followed by Dunnett's test, which is MORE conservative than the unadjusted t-test recomputed here, so the discrepancy can only widen under the authors' own method.

consequence.explanation: The asterisk marking respiration rate as significantly altered at 4 weeks after nerve lesion cannot be produced by the group statistics printed beside it.

findings.location: Table 2, Respiration cycle/min, Nerve Lesion 10 wk (12 ± 8*) vs Control (14 ± 3)
findings.quote: Values are Mean ± SD of 6–8 rats at each point.
findings.notes: Same reasoning and same favourable n=8 assumption as t2_respiration_nl4wk_star. p < 0.05 is unreachable under every standard reading. The Results text asserts 'Respiration rate after nerve lesion in saline treated rats showed significant decrease after 10 weeks', which is the claim this asterisk supports.

findings.quote: Values are Mean ± SD of 6–8 rats at each point.
findings.notes: n=8 per group assumed (top of stated 6-8 range). This is a PRIMARY outcome cell: paw withdrawal latency is one of the two pain measures the abstract's central hyperalgesia claim rests on. p < 0.05 is unreachable under Welch's and Student's, one- or two-tailed, and Dunnett's adjustment would only make it larger.

findings.location: Table 2, Body wt (g), #CBL + NL 10 wk (274 ± 8*) vs Control (267 ± 8)
findings.quote: Values are Mean ± SD of 6–8 rats at each point.
findings.notes: Not an impossibility. The smallest achievable TWO-tailed p over the rounding interval is 0.051 -- just above 0.05 -- so the asterisk is reachable only under a one-tailed test, which the paper never states it used, and only at the extreme corner of the rounding box with n=8 (the top of the stated 6-8 range). At n=6 it would not be reachable two-tailed at all. Recorded as suspicious rather than higher because a one-tailed reading is a legitimate convention the tool accepts.

consequence.explanation: The claim that cerebrolysin significantly raised body weight at 10 weeks survives only under an unstated one-tailed test at the most favourable admissible n.

findings.location: Table 3, Paw Withdrawal Latency (Sec), §CBL + NL + Ag 10 wk (4 ± 3*) vs Control (6 ± 3)
findings.quote: Values are Mean ± SD of 6–8 rats at each point.
findings.notes: Not an impossibility: p < 0.05 is reachable, but only in the extreme corner of the rounding box. At the printed values themselves p = 0.204. The tool's verdict is that the reported precision is too coarse to pin the test down (achievable p spans 0.031 to 0.577), which is the honest description: the asterisk is neither confirmed nor refuted by what the paper prints. The same holds for the identically-valued Table 3 cells NL+Ag 8 wk (4 ± 3*) and NL+Cu 4 wk (4 ± 3*).

consequence.explanation: Three starred primary pain-outcome cells reporting 4 ± 3 against a 6 ± 3 control cannot be adjudicated from the printed precision, so the cerebrolysin and nanoparticle claims resting on them are unverifiable rather than wrong.

findings.location: Table 2, Respiration cycle/min, NL + Al NPs 8 wk (16 ± 3*) vs Control (14 ± 3)
findings.quote: Values are Mean ± SD of 6–8 rats at each point.
findings.notes: Reachable but not pinned: p at the printed values is 0.204, and the achievable interval spans 0.031 to 0.577. The same arithmetic covers the identically-valued NL + Cu 10 wk cell (16 ± 3*). Recorded to document that a further group of starred respiration cells is unverifiable at the printed precision, distinct from the three that are outright unreachable.

findings.location: Results, Physiological Variables paragraph; against Table 2 Arterial pH, NL + Ag NPs 10 wk (7.23 ± 0.06, unstarred) vs Control (7.38 ± 0.04)
findings.quote: The arterial pH exhibited slight decrease in nerve lesioned group with or without nanoparticles intoxication; however, the values were not significantly altered (Table 2).

reported.stated_conclusion: the values were not significantly altered

findings.notes: This is the mirror image of the starred-cell problem: a comparison the paper explicitly calls non-significant, and leaves unstarred, is significant by a wide margin. n was set to 6 per group -- the BOTTOM of the stated 6-8 range, the assumption most favourable to the authors' claim of no difference. The entire achievable p interval is [0.00013, 0.0019], i.e. below 0.002 at every admissible rounding, roughly 25-fold below the paper's own alpha. The tool graded this `suspicious` on its wide-t-interval heuristic; the substantive point is that the whole interval sits below 0.05, so the stated non-significance cannot hold under any rounding or n in range. Note the direction: a pH of 7.23 is a marked acidosis, so this is a real physiological effect the paper reports as absent.

consequence.explanation: The Results sentence stating that arterial pH was 'not significantly altered' is contradicted by Table 2's own means and SDs, which imply p < 0.002.

findings.location: Table 2, NL + Cu NPs 10 wk row: Rectal T °C and PaCO2 Torr cells

inputs.blocking: one block per physiological variable, 18 groups each

One identical pair out of 8089 comparisons. IMPORTANT CAVEAT, which lowers the strength of this finding: the tool infers value spans from the whole table (span_mean 346.77), but these two particular variables both happen to live in the narrow 35-37 range by coincidence of their units, so the true coincidence probability is materially higher than the reported 0.00011. Treat as a copy-paste candidate warranting clarification, not as evidence of fabrication. Capped at `suspicious` per rulebook rule 11; duplication is improbable, never impossible. A first pass with all 144 cells in a single block made 0 comparisons and returned `consistent` -- the finding only appears once the table is blocked by variable, which is recorded here so the negative first result is not mistaken for a clean sweep.

The same caption also contains 'CBK 5 ml/kg' for CBL. This is duplicated boilerplate in a load-bearing sentence: the legend is the only place the Figure 8 quantities are defined, and it names the wrong analyte. findings.location: Table 3, Radiant heat thermal stimulation of tail — Tail Latency (Sec) 52 °C, Control and Sham rows
findings.reproduction: not independently reproducible via CLI: no validated tool applies; manual reading of Table 3 via `metascience get-table <xml> 3`
findings.notes: ASSUMPTION-DEPENDENT and therefore capped well below any impossibility claim. The paper states no cut-off time, so this rests on an EXTERNAL benchmark not given in the paper: normal rat tail-flick latency to a ~52 °C radiant stimulus is a few seconds, and cut-offs of roughly 10-15 s are conventional precisely to avoid tissue injury. A 60-64 s control latency would mean uninjured animals held their tails in a noxious 52 °C stimulus for a full minute. No forensic tool applies to this -- it is a domain-plausibility observation, not arithmetic, and it is recorded as such. Note the internal contrast: nerve-lesioned animals in the same column reach 2-4 s, a 15- to 30-fold difference, which is far outside the dynamic range such an assay normally shows.

consequence.explanation: If the control tail-flick latencies are mis-scaled or mis-transcribed, the thermal hyperalgesia effect size that the abstract reports is not interpretable in the stated units.

findings.location: Whole paper (Statistical Treatment section; Tables 2-6; Figures 2, 5, 8)
findings.quote: ANOVA followed by Dunnett’s test for multiple group comparison was done using one control group using commercial software StatView 5 (Abacus Concept, USA) on a Macintosh computer in Classic Environment. A p-value less than 0.05 was considered significant.
findings.notes: statcheck recovered ZERO NHST statistics from the entire paper. This is not a tool failure -- it is an accurate description of the reporting. The paper contains no F statistic, no t statistic, no degrees of freedom and no exact p-value anywhere; every one of its several hundred inferential claims is carried by an asterisk in a table cell or a figure. The consequence is that no reported test statistic can be recalculated against its own p-value, and the only route to checking any claim is reconstruction from the group means and SDs, which is what the rivets_independent_t findings above do. Severity is `indeterminate` because nothing could be verified, not because the paper passed a check.

consequence.explanation: Every inferential claim in the paper is unauditable by direct recalculation; all verification must go through reconstruction from descriptives.

findings.location: Table 3 footnote; family = 17 non-control groups x 3 pain measures
findings.quote: *P < 0.05; **P < 0.01 from control group, #P < 0.05 from Nerve lesion, ANOVA followed by Dunnett’s test for multiple group comparison from one group.

inputs.family_label: Table 3: all group-vs-control comparisons across the three pain measures

reported.stated_correction: Dunnett's test, within each ANOVA, against one control group

computed.note: no uncorrected tests -- all 51 were dropped because their p-values are thresholds rather than exact values

findings.reproduction: metascience multiplicity --family-label 'Table 3 group-vs-control comparisons across three pain measures' --tests '[{"id":"t3_1","p_value":0.05,"p_is_threshold":true,"correction_applied":"none"}]' --alpha 0.05
findings.notes: The multiplicity arithmetic cannot be run on this paper at all, and the reason is worth stating plainly: the tool drops thresholded p-values rather than coercing them, and every p-value in this paper is a threshold. So no family-wise error rate, no Benjamini-Hochberg count, and no surviving-claims interval can be computed. What can be said without arithmetic is the scale: Tables 2-6 alone print on the order of 500 group-versus-control comparisons against a single shared control group (136 + 51 + 102 + 112 + 112), plus three figure panels, and the stated Dunnett's adjustment operates only within a single measure -- it does not span the 8 variables of Table 2, the 3 measures of Table 3, or the five tables. Recorded as `indeterminate`, since a refusal is the result here and must not be read as either a pass or a quantified failure.

consequence.explanation: How many of the paper's several hundred asterisked claims would survive correction across measures cannot be determined from what is printed.

findings.location: Table 3 (Von Frey / paw withdrawal / tail flick), all 54 printed cells
findings.quote: Values are Mean ± SD of 6–8 rats at each point. For simplicity, the values are adjusted to nearest numbers.

inputs.bindings: all rows bound to a single continuous pain-measure variable

computed.refusal_reason: check_sd_or_se needs n and this cell carries none

findings.notes: All 54 cells were typed successfully (100% parse coverage, every cell mean_sd), and then ZERO checks ran: 54 of 54 refused. Two independent reasons, both structural. First, the outcome variables are continuous (withdrawal weight in grams, latency in seconds), which correctly bars GRIM, GRIMMER, SPRITE and DEBIT -- applying them here would manufacture impossibilities out of ordinary measurements. Second, the paper never states an exact n for any cell, only the range '6-8 rats at each point', so even the dispersion checks cannot be pinned. This is the denominator that matters for the whole review: the tables of this paper are, by construction, almost entirely immune to per-cell forensic arithmetic, and the significance-reconstruction route used elsewhere in this sweep is the only one available. The same reasoning applies unchanged to Tables 2, 4, 5 and 6, whose variables are likewise all continuous and whose footnotes state the same 6-8 range.

consequence.explanation: No per-cell granularity check can be run anywhere in this paper's five results tables, so absence of such findings is not evidence the values are sound.

Under rulebook rule 7 this is a state-but-withhold pattern. It is a weak signal on its own and is recorded as such; its relevance here is that it closes off the one route that could resolve the discrepancies found above -- the underlying per-animal values would settle the Table 1 accounting and every unreachable-p asterisk at once. The paper also supplies no supplementary materials of any kind, so no participant-level duplication analysis was possible.

consequence.explanation: None of the numeric discrepancies identified in this sweep can be resolved by a reader, because the underlying data are not available.

unchecked.location: Figures 2, 5 and 8 (neuronal injury counts, albumin-positive cell counts, GFAP-positive cell counts)
unchecked.reason: These three figures carry group means, SDs and significance markers for 6-8 rats per point that appear NOWHERE in the text or in any table -- they are the sole source for the neuronal-injury, albumin-immunoreactivity and GFAP-immunoreactivity results, and each supports claims made in the abstract. Figure extraction was not run and no values were digitized. Anything read off these plots would carry figure_pixels provenance and would in any case be barred from GRIM/GRIMMER/SPRITE/DEBIT. This is a real hole in the coverage of this review, not a formality: a substantial block of the paper's inferential claims was not examined at all.

unchecked.location: Table 4, Volume Swelling (%f) columns (T10-11 and L5-S2), all rows
unchecked.reason: Volume swelling is a DERIVED quantity: 'volume swelling (%ƒ) was calculated from the changes of water content as described earlier'. The paper cites a prior method but never states the transformation, so the mapping from the water-content column to the swelling column is not reproducible from anything printed here. Checking it would require assuming a conversion factor the paper does not give, which rulebook rule 4 forbids. The column also carries no SDs and no significance markers, so no dispersion or test check applies.

unchecked.location: Tables 2, 4, 5 and 6 -- per-cell granularity checks
unchecked.reason: Not run individually, for the same two structural reasons established by the check_table run on Table 3 (finding table3_typed_cells_all_refused): every variable in these tables is a continuous physiological or biochemical measure, which correctly bars GRIM/GRIMMER/SPRITE/DEBIT, and every footnote states n only as a range ('6-8 rats at each point'), which bars the dispersion checks. Running check_table on each would return the same 100% refusal; the Table 3 run is recorded as the representative denominator rather than repeated four times.

unchecked.location: Exact per-cell sample sizes throughout Tables 2-6 and Figures 2, 5, 8
unchecked.reason: The paper states n only as '6-8 rats at each point' (and Table 5's footnote is corrupted to 'of–8 rats'). No cell carries its own n. Every significance recalculation in this sweep therefore had to assume a value; n=8 was used where the aim was to test a significance claim (most favourable to the authors) and n=6 where the aim was to test a non-significance claim (likewise most favourable), and each finding names which was used.

unchecked.location: Remaining starred comparisons in Tables 2, 4, 5 and 6 (on the order of 450 cells)
unchecked.reason: Eleven comparisons were reconstructed individually, selected as those with the smallest mean differences relative to their SDs -- i.e. where a significance claim was most likely to be unsupportable. The remaining cells were not individually recalculated. The four unreachable-p results should therefore be read as a floor on the number of unsupportable asterisks in this paper, established by a targeted rather than an exhaustive search, not as a count of them.

unchecked.location: Supplementary materials / participant-level data
unchecked.reason: None are provided with the article. The Data Availability statement reads only 'Enquiries about data availability should be directed to the authors.' No spreadsheet or deposited dataset exists to run detect_raw_duplication against, so the strongest available data-integrity check could not be attempted. Recorded as 'not provided', which is distinct from 'present but unreadable'.

unchecked.location: Retraction notice and its stated grounds
unchecked.reason: The version of record is titled 'RETRACTED ARTICLE' but the retraction notice itself was not among the supplied files. The reasons the publisher gave are therefore unknown to this sweep, and no finding here is derived from or should be read as reconstructing them.

unchecked.location: Baseline-similarity testing (csf_test, bayesian_table1_dispersion)
unchecked.reason: Deliberately not run. These methods test whether randomised arms are more similar at baseline than allocation allows. This is a non-randomised laboratory experiment with deliberately constructed treatment groups and no baseline table of randomised arms, so the null the tests assume does not exist here and any verdict would be meaningless.

unchecked.location: GRIM-U / rank-sum granularity checks
unchecked.reason: Deliberately not run. The paper attributes every comparison to ANOVA with Dunnett's test; no Mann-Whitney or Wilcoxon rank-sum test is reported anywhere. Applying GRIM-U to ANOVA p-values is the toolkit's single most likely route to a false accusation, and it is gated by the analyst, not the tool.

unchecked.location: Discussion sections (sections 30-37) and reference list
unchecked.reason: Read only via the whole-PDF statcheck sweep, which found no test statistics anywhere in the document. Not examined line by line for citation or textual anomalies beyond the figure captions and load-bearing Results sentences reported above.

findings.location: Table 1 (Experimental Protocol in Nerve Lesion), row Total column
findings.quote: Experiments were carried out on 348 male albino Wistar Rats
findings.notes: Run via check_summation_batch (23 sums in one call). 3 of 18 per-group row totals in Table 1 exceed the sum of their own three assay-stream cells by exactly 2 animals each. The remaining 15 rows reconcile exactly. Animal counts must hold exactly, so tolerance was set to 0. The constant +2 offset in all three failures is consistent with transcription/editing error rather than a random arithmetic slip, but the direction always over-states the number of animals.

consequence.explanation: The per-group n that every significance test in Tables 2-6 depends on cannot be pinned down for these three groups, since the table gives two different answers for each.

findings.location: Table 1, Grand Total row against the assay columns above it

findings.notes: Two of the three printed column Grand Totals are LOWER than the sum of the cells printed above them (106 vs 114; 112 vs 118). The Biochemical Analyses column reconciles exactly. Note the direction is opposite to the row-total errors, which over-state; these under-state.

consequence.explanation: The number of animals contributing to the physiological/pain measurements (Tables 2 and 3) and to the BSCB measurements (Table 4) is stated two ways that differ by 8 and 6 animals respectively.

findings.location: Table 1 grand total and Animals section ('348 male albino Wistar Rats')
findings.quote: Experiments were carried out on 348 male albino Wistar Rats

comparisons: vs sum of the 18 printed row Totals = 368

findings.notes: The paper's animal accounting yields THREE mutually inconsistent totals: the individual cells of Table 1 sum to 362; the printed per-group Total column sums to 368; and both the stated text figure and the printed Grand Total cell say 348. Only the last two agree with each other, and they agree only because 106 + 112 + 130 = 348 -- i.e. the grand total is internally consistent with the (incorrect) column totals rather than with the animals actually listed. All three numbers cannot describe the same experiment.

consequence.explanation: The headline sample size of the study -- 348 rats -- is not recoverable from the paper's own allocation table, which accounts for either 362 or 368 animals depending on which printed figures are added.

findings.location: Table 2, Respiration cycle/min, Nerve Lesion 4 wk (12 ± 9*) vs Control (14 ± 3)
findings.quote: Values are Mean ± SD of 6–8 rats at each point.
findings.notes: n was set to 8 per group, the TOP of the paper's stated 6-8 range, which is the assumption most favourable to the authors' significance claim; at n=6 the p-values would be larger still. The achievable two-tailed p across the entire rounding interval implied by the printed 0-decimal means and SDs is [0.354, 0.786], and one-tailed [0.177, 0.393]. p < 0.05 is unreachable under Welch's and Student's tests, one- or two-tailed. The paper's stated analysis was ANOVA followed by Dunnett's test, which is MORE conservative than the unadjusted t-test recomputed here, so the discrepancy can only widen under the authors' own method.

consequence.explanation: The asterisk marking respiration rate as significantly altered at 4 weeks after nerve lesion cannot be produced by the group statistics printed beside it.

findings.location: Table 2, Body wt (g), #CBL + NL 10 wk (274 ± 8*) vs Control (267 ± 8)

findings.notes: Not an impossibility. findings.location: Results, Physiological Variables paragraph; against Table 2 Arterial pH, NL + Ag NPs 10 wk (7.23 ± 0.06, unstarred) vs Control (7.38 ± 0.04)
findings.quote: The arterial pH exhibited slight decrease in nerve lesioned group with or without nanoparticles intoxication; however, the values were not significantly altered (Table 2).

reported.stated_conclusion: the values were not significantly altered

findings.notes: This is the mirror image of the starred-cell problem: a comparison the paper explicitly calls non-significant, and leaves unstarred, is significant by a wide margin. n was set to 6 per group -- the BOTTOM of the stated 6-8 range, the assumption most favourable to the authors' claim of no difference. The entire achievable p interval is [0.00013, 0.0019], i.e. below 0.002 at every admissible rounding, roughly 25-fold below the paper's own alpha. The tool graded this `suspicious` on its wide-t-interval heuristic; the substantive point is that the whole interval sits below 0.05, so the stated non-significance cannot hold under any rounding or n in range. Note the direction: a pH of 7.23 is a marked acidosis, so this is a real physiological effect the paper reports as absent.

consequence.explanation: The Results sentence stating that arterial pH was 'not significantly altered' is contradicted by Table 2's own means and SDs, which imply p < 0.002.

findings.location: Table 3, Radiant heat thermal stimulation of tail — Tail Latency (Sec) 52 °C, Control and Sham rows
findings.reproduction: not independently reproducible as a CLI check -- no validated tool applies to a domain-plausibility judgement; re-read the values via `metascience get-table /mnt/c/Users/gregs/agent_for_forensic_metascience/cerebrolysin_run_2026-08-09/10.1007--s11064-023-03861-8/10.1007--s11064-023-03861-8.xml 3`
findings.notes: ASSUMPTION-DEPENDENT and therefore deliberately capped well below any impossibility claim. The paper states no cut-off time, so this rests on an EXTERNAL benchmark not given in the paper: normal rat tail-flick latency to a ~52 °C radiant stimulus is a few seconds, and cut-offs of roughly 10-15 s are conventional precisely to avoid tissue injury. A 60-64 s control latency would mean uninjured animals held their tails in a noxious 52 °C stimulus for a full minute. No forensic tool applies -- this is a domain-plausibility observation, not arithmetic, and is recorded as such rather than dressed up as a computation. Note the internal contrast: nerve-lesioned animals in the same column reach 2-4 s, a 15- to 30-fold difference, far outside the dynamic range such an assay normally shows.

consequence.explanation: If the control tail-flick latencies are mis-scaled or mis-transcribed, the thermal hyperalgesia effect size that the abstract reports is not interpretable in the stated units.

findings.location: Whole paper (Statistical Treatment section; Tables 2-6; Figures 2, 5, 8)
findings.quote: ANOVA followed by Dunnett’s test for multiple group comparison was done using one control group using commercial software StatView 5 (Abacus Concept, USA) on a Macintosh computer in Classic Environment. A p-value less than 0.05 was considered significant.
findings.notes: statcheck recovered ZERO NHST statistics from the entire paper. This is not a tool failure -- it is an accurate description of the reporting. The paper contains no F statistic, no t statistic, no degrees of freedom and no exact p-value anywhere; every one of its several hundred inferential claims is carried by an asterisk in a table cell or a figure. The consequence is that no reported test statistic can be recalculated against its own p-value, and the only route to checking any claim is reconstruction from the group means and SDs, which is what the rivets_independent_t findings above do. Severity is `indeterminate` because nothing could be verified, NOT because the paper passed a check.

consequence.explanation: Every inferential claim in the paper is unauditable by direct recalculation; all verification must go through reconstruction from descriptives.

findings.notes: The multiplicity arithmetic cannot be run on this paper at all, and the reason is worth stating plainly: the tool drops thresholded p-values rather than coercing them, and every p-value in this paper is a threshold. So no family-wise error rate, no Benjamini-Hochberg count, and no surviving-claims interval can be computed. What can be said without arithmetic is the scale: Tables 2-6 alone print on the order of 500 group-versus-control comparisons against a single shared control group (136 + 51 + 102 + 112 + 112), plus three figure panels, and the stated Dunnett's adjustment operates only within a single measure -- it does not span the 8 variables of Table 2, the 3 measures of Table 3, or the five tables. Recorded as `indeterminate`, since a refusal is the result here and must not be read as either a pass or a quantified failure.

consequence.explanation: How many of the paper's several hundred asterisked claims would survive correction across measures cannot be determined from what is printed.

findings.location: Table 3 (Von Frey / paw withdrawal / tail flick), all 54 printed cells
findings.quote: Values are Mean ± SD of 6–8 rats at each point. For simplicity, the values are adjusted to nearest numbers.

inputs.bindings: all rows bound to a single continuous pain-measure variable

computed.refusal_reason: check_sd_or_se needs n and this cell carries none

findings.notes: Run via check_table, which typed all 54 cells successfully (100% parse coverage, every cell mean_sd) and then dispatched to check_sd_or_se -- the only applicable check -- which refused on all 54. Two independent structural reasons. First, the outcome variables are continuous (withdrawal weight in grams, latency in seconds), which correctly bars GRIM, GRIMMER, SPRITE and DEBIT; applying them here would manufacture impossibilities out of ordinary measurements. Second, the paper never states an exact n for any cell, only the range '6-8 rats at each point', so even the dispersion check cannot be pinned. This is the denominator that matters for the whole review: 0 of 54 checks could run. The tables of this paper are by construction almost entirely immune to per-cell forensic arithmetic, and the significance-reconstruction route used elsewhere in this sweep is the only one available. The same reasoning applies unchanged to Tables 2, 4, 5 and 6, whose variables are likewise all continuous and whose footnotes state the same 6-8 range.

consequence.explanation: No per-cell granularity check can be run anywhere in this paper's five results tables, so the absence of such findings is not evidence the values are sound.

The retraction notice itself was not among the supplied files, so the stated grounds for retraction are unknown to this sweep and NOTHING in this review should be read as reconstructing or endorsing them. The findings above were derived independently from the paper's own numbers and stand or fall on their own.

consequence.explanation: Bears on how the paper's claims should be cited, but does not itself establish anything about the numbers checked here.

unchecked.location: Figures 2, 5 and 8 (neuronal injury counts, albumin-positive cell counts, GFAP-positive cell counts)
unchecked.reason: These three figures carry group means, SDs and significance markers for 6-8 rats per point that appear NOWHERE in the text or in any table -- they are the sole source for the neuronal-injury, albumin-immunoreactivity and GFAP-immunoreactivity results, and each supports claims made in the abstract. Figure extraction was not run and no values were digitized. Anything read off these plots would carry figure_pixels provenance and would in any case be barred from GRIM/GRIMMER/SPRITE/DEBIT. This is a real hole in the coverage of this review, not a formality: a substantial block of the paper's inferential claims was not examined at all.

unchecked.location: Table 4, Volume Swelling (%f) columns (T10-11 and L5-S2), all rows
unchecked.reason: Volume swelling is a DERIVED quantity: 'volume swelling (%ƒ) was calculated from the changes of water content as described earlier'. The paper cites a prior method but never states the transformation, so the mapping from the water-content column to the swelling column is not reproducible from anything printed here. Checking it would require assuming a conversion factor the paper does not give, which rulebook rule 4 forbids. The column also carries no SDs and no significance markers, so no dispersion or test check applies.

unchecked.location: Tables 2, 4, 5 and 6 -- per-cell granularity checks
unchecked.reason: Not run individually, for the same two structural reasons established by the check_table run on Table 3 (finding table3_typed_cells_all_refused): every variable in these tables is a continuous physiological or biochemical measure, which correctly bars GRIM/GRIMMER/SPRITE/DEBIT, and every footnote states n only as a range ('6-8 rats at each point'), which bars the dispersion checks. Running check_table on each would return the same 100% refusal; the Table 3 run is recorded as the representative denominator rather than repeated four times.

unchecked.location: Exact per-cell sample sizes throughout Tables 2-6 and Figures 2, 5, 8
unchecked.reason: The paper states n only as '6-8 rats at each point' (and Table 5's footnote is corrupted to 'of–8 rats'). No cell carries its own n. Every significance recalculation in this sweep therefore had to assume a value; n=8 was used where the aim was to test a significance claim (most favourable to the authors) and n=6 where the aim was to test a non-significance claim (likewise most favourable), and each finding names which was used.

unchecked.location: Remaining starred comparisons in Tables 2, 4, 5 and 6 (on the order of 450 cells)
unchecked.reason: Eleven comparisons were reconstructed individually, selected as those with the smallest mean differences relative to their SDs -- i.e. where a significance claim was most likely to be unsupportable. The remaining cells were not individually recalculated. The four unreachable-p results should therefore be read as a FLOOR on the number of unsupportable asterisks in this paper, established by a targeted rather than an exhaustive search, not as a count of them.

unchecked.location: Supplementary materials / participant-level data
unchecked.reason: None are provided with the article. The Data Availability statement reads only 'Enquiries about data availability should be directed to the authors.' No spreadsheet or deposited dataset exists to run detect_raw_duplication against, so the strongest available data-integrity check could not be attempted. Recorded as 'not provided', which is distinct from 'present but unreadable'.

unchecked.location: Retraction notice and its stated grounds
unchecked.reason: The version of record is titled 'RETRACTED ARTICLE' but the retraction notice itself was not among the supplied files. The reasons the publisher gave are therefore unknown to this sweep, and no finding here is derived from or should be read as reconstructing them.

unchecked.location: Baseline-similarity testing (csf_test, bayesian_table1_dispersion)
unchecked.reason: Deliberately not run. These methods test whether randomised arms are more similar at baseline than allocation allows. This is a non-randomised laboratory experiment with deliberately constructed treatment groups and no baseline table of randomised arms, so the null the tests assume does not exist here and any verdict would be meaningless.

unchecked.location: GRIM-U / rank-sum granularity checks
unchecked.reason: Deliberately not run. The paper attributes every comparison to ANOVA with Dunnett's test; no Mann-Whitney or Wilcoxon rank-sum test is reported anywhere. Applying GRIM-U to ANOVA p-values is the toolkit's single most likely route to a false accusation, and it is gated by the analyst, not the tool.

unchecked.location: Duplication scanning of Tables 3, 4, 5 and 6 against each other and against Table 2
unchecked.reason: Only Table 2 was scanned (144 cells, 8 blocks, 8089 comparisons). Cross-table scanning was not run because the tables report entirely different physical quantities in different units on partly different animals (Table 1 allocates distinct animals to the physiological, BSCB and biochemical streams), so a cross-table match would be hard to interpret and the tool's span model -- already noted as over-confident within Table 2 -- would be less reliable still. A within-table scan of Tables 4, 5 and 6 remains a reasonable further check that was not performed.

unchecked.location: Discussion sections (sections 30-37) and reference list
unchecked.reason: Read only via the whole-PDF statcheck sweep, which found no test statistics anywhere in the document. Not examined line by line for citation or textual anomalies beyond the figure captions and load-bearing Results sentences reported above.
